OpenRouter is officially part of @stripe today!
More than 10 million developers and companies use OpenRouter, and as they build with more models across more workloads, they need control over what it costs and where their data goes.
OpenRouter has built that operating infrastructure to help run AI across every model and provider, with access to new models, uptime through outages, and enforced spend and data policies for each team.
Joining Stripe, which has spent years running critical infrastructure for businesses around the world, means we can build it faster and support companies at every scale.
Our commitment to neutrality stays the same. Models and providers compete on quality, reliability, and price. You decide what works for your business.
Stripe (@stripe)
OpenRouter is now part of Stripe.
Stripe is building the economic infrastructure for AI. Together with OpenRouter, we’ll help businesses explore new models and optimize token routing and usage.

Providers’ data-handling claims have mostly relied on self-attestation. This isn't going to be sufficient.
Just as continuous benchmarking and monitoring transformed the quality and reliability of inference both on and out of OpenRouter, we expect technical validation, auditing, and continuous testing to do the same for data policy enforcement.
Encrypted TEE (Trusted Execution Environment) inference will be a great way for providers to accelerate this.
We will keep raising the bar, and providers that want to be on OpenRouter will need to meet it.
OpenRouter (@OpenRouter)
Security researchers recently found data-handling problems with some inference providers available on OpenRouter. The findings showed no breach of OpenRouter itself.
In response, we’ve off-boarded 3 providers, removed many endpoints from ZDR eligibility, and notified affected customers.
We’re now building the researchers’ testing into ongoing checks. Full update and provider write-ups on our blog:
— https://x.com/OpenRouter/status/2124315081899200715
items.title_ja:
プロバイダーのデータ処理に関する主張は、ほとんどが自己証明に依存しています。これでは十分ではありません。
継続的なベンチマークとモニタリングによって OpenRouter 内外の推論の品質と信頼性が変化したのと同様に、データ ポリシーの適用に関しても技術的な検証、監査、継続的なテストが同様の効果をもたらすことを期待しています。
暗号化された TEE (信頼された実行環境) 推論は、プロバイダーにとってこれを加速する優れた方法になります。
私たちは基準を引き上げ続け、OpenRouter への参加を希望するプロバイダーはその基準を満たす必要があります。
オープンルーター (@OpenRouter)
セキュリティ研究者は最近、OpenRouter で利用できる一部の推論プロバイダーでデータ処理の問題を発見しました。調査結果では、OpenRouter 自体の侵害は認められませんでした。
これに応じて、私たちは 3 つのプロバイダーをオフボードし、多くのエンドポイントを ZDR 資格から削除し、影響を受ける顧客に通知しました。
私たちは現在、研究者によるテストを継続的なチェックに組み込んでいます。完全なアップデートとプロバイダーの記事はブログにあります。
— https://x.com/OpenRouter/status/2124315081899200715

Robots look impressive in demos, but move one object or change the lighting and a lot of them fall apart.
Embo, the new company from the team behind Dreamer and VideoGPT, just came out of stealth to work on exactly that. They raised $110M led by a16z, the largest seed round in robotics history.
Their approach is a world model trained on huge amounts of internet video and robot demos. The robot brain then practices skills inside that model, across imagined scenarios, and learns from its failures without breaking anything in the real world.
If this works, robots can learn from far more experience than anyone could ever collect on real hardware. That would be a big deal for the whole field.
Danijar Hafner (@danijar)
I'm excited to introduce Embo!
We are building the brain for intelligent robots to help people around the world.
We believe intelligent robots will unlock an era of abundance, making goods and services affordable for everybody. But to deploy them at scale, robots need to work out of the box in unfamiliar scenarios. At Embo, we are building frontier AI models with a deep understanding of physical reality and fine-grained motor skills.
Today's robot skills are fragile. Demonstrations can teach repetitive behaviors, but they cannot cover every object or situation a robot will encounter. We need general pretraining at internet scale to fill the gaps between individual tasks and practice to develop reliable motor skills.
The world models our team has pioneered unlock a path to general robots. Our robot brain pretrains on massive amounts of internet video to learn about objects, physical interactions, and how tasks unfold. It then practices motor skills in diverse imagined scenarios to become robust to unexpected situations.
Our team is behind seminal work in AI including Dreamer, VideoGPT, and Diffusion Forcing, with experience from DeepMind, Meta Superintelligence Labs, NVIDIA Cosmos, Berkeley, and MIT.
We have raised a $110M Seed led by @a16z. We are excited to partner with them, @khoslaventures, DST Global, NVentures (@nvidia), @strikervp, and other strategic investors to bring reliable intelligent robots out into the world.

I dont know if this post helped Jensen at all, probably not. But at least im proud of myself of always standing with Jensen, never trusted that campaign against him and didn't share that smear campaign.
Jensen is a good person. And today is good day for all of us.
Chubby♨️ (@kimmonismus)
Right now, the media is full of stories that paint Jensen Huang in a bad light. I have actually met Jensen, and I want to tell you a story. (1/2)
My interview with Jensen hasn't been published yet, which is probably understandable given the current situation. More on that when the time is right. But I had the chance to meet Jensen Huang in person several times while traveling through Europe with NVIDIA, and I want to tell you about it, especially about one experience that has stayed with me.
Some quick background: NVIDIA invited me to join Jensen's European tour last month, together with Bloomberg and Steve Nouri. We were there for every stop: Paris, London, Stockholm, Berlin. I was on site for every one of his public speeches.
A lot is being said right now about Jensen making statements that many find contemptible, while others take them with humor. And to be fair, Jensen does have a slightly edgy humor that rubs some people the wrong way. He speaks plainly, says what he thinks and makes jokes that can offend, but he always makes fun of himself too.
And I, at least, can say one thing very clearly: never once did I feel that any of his remarks were meant as an attack, as belittling or as humiliating. It was always situational comedy. If Jensen hadn't been CEO of NVIDIA, he would have made an outstanding stand-up comedian, always ready with a quip. But as we all know, that's a matter of taste, and saying that I always found it amusing won't calm anyone down.
So here are two stories that show Jensen really has a good heart, and that the campaign against him distorts his image.
This is my personal experience:
NVIDIA gave me the opportunity to do a 30-minute interview with Jensen in Stockholm.
As you can imagine, I was incredibly nervous. Honestly, I was even scared. Me, a small "content creator," getting to meet Jensen in person and talk to him. He makes time even for little people like me. I met him and his staff at a café in Stockholm. We went inside and, as was bound to happen, my camera gear fell out of my backpack onto the floor. My stress level: through the roof. But Jensen stayed calm and relaxed, told me everything was fine and that I didn't need to stress, and put his hand on my shoulder. Not one snide word, no making fun of me. Quite the opposite. He knew I was genuinely stressed and helped me relax.
Then we started the interview. And while we were talking, people kept coming into the café where we were recording. It was a café open to the public. And as you'd expect, the same thing happened again and again: while Jensen and I were talking, guests recognized him and more or less burst into our interview. And Jensen took time for every single one of them. Not one bad word, no irritation, no stupid remark. He gave every guest his time, took photos, had conversations. In the middle of the interview. I was surprised and genuinely moved. No arrogance on his part, just friendly humanity. And that's how an interview scheduled for 30 minutes turned into 60. Simply because Jensen and I had such a good conversation and he kindly gave all those guests extra time on top.
But the most impressive part actually came afterwards. We had been eating a Swedish pastry, it's called “fika” (at least that’s how we called it). And Jensen loved it. After we wrapped up the interview, Jensen went to the trunk of his car, grabbed some cash, went back into the café and bought “fika” for everyone. For himself, his security, his staff, for everyone.
No camera recorded it. Nothing done purely for PR. Nothing meant to make him "look better." Just a human gesture, because he liked the pastry and wanted everyone to enjoy it too. If I hadn't told this story today, it would never have been told. And to me it shows that Jensen is a genuinely good person.
I gain nothing from writing this. Jensen is no longer CEO. And nobody suggested I write this story down.
